reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive platelet disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of the glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor
It produces a mucocutaneous bleeding tendency together with mild thrombocytopenia and characteristically large (giant) platelets on the film
The triad of thrombocytopenia, giant platelets and a mucocutaneous bleeding history should prompt consideration of the diagnosis
The distinctive aggregometry pattern is absent agglutination to ristocetin that is not corrected by adding normal plasma, with preserved aggregation to other physiological agonists
This ristocetin pattern is the mirror image of Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where ristocetin response is preserved but other agonist responses are absent
Diagnosis is confirmed by reduced glycoprotein Ib-IX-V expression on flow cytometry and by GP1BA, GP1BB or GP9 genetic testing
Management uses local measures, antifibrinolytics, desmopressin in some settings and platelet transfusion for significant bleeding, mindful of alloimmunisation risk
reference.pathophysiology: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in GP1BA, GP1BB or GP9, which encode subunits of the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex. This complex is the receptor through which platelets bind von Willebrand factor on exposed subendothelium, the first step of platelet adhesion under high shear. When the complex is deficient or defective, platelets cannot tether to the vessel wall, so primary haemostasis is impaired. The same molecular defect disturbs normal megakaryocyte and platelet development, producing mild thrombocytopenia and abnormally large platelets, and the combined adhesion failure and low platelet number underlie the bleeding phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited macrothrombocytopenias (for example MYH9-related disease)
Platelet secretion or storage pool defects
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film showing thrombocytopenia with giant platelets
Platelet aggregometry demonstrating absent ristocetin-induced agglutination not corrected by normal plasma
Flow cytometry for glycoprotein Ib-IX-V expression
Von Willebrand studies to exclude von Willebrand disease
Review of the film to exclude pseudothrombocytopenia and other macrothrombocytopenias
Genetic testing of GP1BA, GP1BB and GP9
redFlags: Major haemorrhage such as gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding
Severe menorrhagia or postpartum bleeding with haemodynamic compromise
reference.prognosis: With appropriate supportive care and bleeding prophylaxis around procedures, most patients do well, although serious spontaneous or provoked bleeds can occur and repeated transfusion carries a risk of alloimmunisation.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the low platelet count as immune thrombocytopenia and treating with immunosuppression
Automated analysers undercounting the giant platelets, exaggerating the apparent thrombocytopenia
Confusing the ristocetin defect with von Willebrand disease without a mixing (normal plasma) study
Overusing platelet transfusion and provoking alloimmunisation
management: Use local pressure and antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid as first-line for mucocutaneous and menstrual bleeding
Trial desmopressin for minor bleeding where a response is documented, recognising it is less reliable than in some other platelet disorders
Transfuse platelets for major or refractory bleeding and surgical cover, favouring leucodepleted HLA-matched units to reduce alloimmunisation
Consider recombinant activated factor VII for bleeds unresponsive to platelets or in alloimmunised patients
Avoid aspirin and other antiplatelet and NSAID agents and correct iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic loss
Plan haematology review ahead of surgery, childbirth or invasive procedures with a defined haemostatic strategy
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive GP1BA, GP1BB or GP9 disorder and offer family testing
